regime_line: Strong economic data undid Wednesday's rate relief in a single day: the 30-year Treasury yield is back up to 5.23% — higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months — and that, not anything in credit or corporate health, is what's pressuring stocks; Walmart's weakest sales growth in six-plus years is the new question mark.
provenance_note: Movers stated-reasons via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): Reuters/Investing.com, Bloomberg, Seeking Alpha, Babypips, Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq.com, GuruFocus.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — checking our own work

This section grades what the brief said on earlier days. Three predictions are still open; one new one gets logged today.

  • CL-0001 — Wednesday we said: if the Fed minutes sounded hawkish, long rates would push past Monday's high (5.31%) within two days. Deadline is today's close. So far it's failing — Thursday closed at 5.23%, still 8bp short — and notably, it's failing even though the test got its best shot: Thursday's data was hot, and long rates still recovered only half of Wednesday's drop. Final grade in Monday's brief.
  • CL-0002 — Tuesday we said: the AI-chip selloff was about rising rates, not about doubts in AI demand. The test: chip stocks (SMH) can't keep badly lagging the market. Thursday supported it — chips actually rose 0.31% while the overall market fell 0.84%. If the selling had been about AI demand, they'd fall on any kind of day. Two of five days in; due Tuesday.
  • CL-0003 — we said: the rise in long rates is about the price of lending long-term, not about inflation fear. The check: inflation expectations (the 10-year "breakeven") stay quiet. They have — 2.30%, barely moved all week, even as yields swung. Holding; due Tuesday.
  • CL-0004 (new, due 08-28): Walmart's weak quarter might mean the broader consumer is softening — or it might be Walmart's own problem. The test: if consumers are really pulling back, the consumer-discretionary sector (XLY) should lag the market by at least 1.5 points over the next five days. Deere and Estée Lauder beat the same week, which is why this is logged as a question, not a conclusion.
story_html:
Thursday's economic data came in strong — and right now, strong data is bad news for bonds. Jobless claims were 206,000, fewer layoffs than expected (Reuters/Investing.com), and the Philadelphia Fed's factory survey printed 47.4 against expectations near 24 — a blowout (Babypips). Why that matters: strong data means no reason for the Fed to cut, and more growth to finance — so investors demand higher yields on long-term bonds. The 30-year Treasury rose back to 5.23%, undoing half of Wednesday's buyback-driven relief in one session. In real-life terms, the rate that anchors everything long-term — mortgage pricing, annuity payouts, the value of long bond funds — is being set day-to-day by the economic data, and this week the data ran hot.

Stocks fell broadly (S&P 500 −0.87%, small caps −1.34%), and in a different way than earlier this week: Tuesday and Wednesday had clear winners and losers as money rotated between sectors; Thursday, for the first time since this system began tracking it, no sector stood apart from the pack — everyone sold a little of everything. The headline casualty was Walmart, down 9.15% after reporting its slowest quarterly sales growth in more than six years (Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq.com). That's the week's first genuinely concerning consumer signal — the country's biggest retailer, closest to the average household. But the very same week, Estée Lauder and Deere both beat expectations, so the brief logs the "consumer is softening" idea as a claim to test (CL-0004 above) rather than a conclusion to repeat.

Now the surprise: the AI-chip stocks that got hammered earlier this week went up on a down day — the semiconductor index gained 0.31% while the market fell, with Lumentum +6.25% and Marvell +5.79%. If Tuesday's selling had really been about doubts in AI demand, these stocks would fall regardless of the market's direction; rising while everything else sinks looks instead like the earlier selling was a crowded trade being unwound. And the market's smoke detector stayed silent: junk-bond spreads — the extra yield investors demand to lend to risky companies, usually the first thing to jump when something is genuinely breaking — sat near their calmest levels of the year (2.73%). Put together: this week isn't a crisis story. It's the market renegotiating, in public, what it costs to borrow money for decades.
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-08-20 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, and both credit-spread series publish a day behind (§5); the Fed balance sheet and TGA are weekly (08-19). Flagged rows (⚑): the level is far outside its past-6-months normal range (|z| ≥ 1.5) — see the Reading key at the bottom.
dashboard_interp_html: The whole week happened in one row of this table. The 30-year yield went 5.31 → 5.19 → 5.23 in three sessions: up on fear of too much long-term bond supply, down when the Treasury said it would buy some of that supply back, back up on Thursday's hot data. Meanwhile the 2-year — the rate that tracks what the Fed will actually do — didn't move at all (4.19% every single day). Translation: markets aren't debating the Fed's next move; they're debating how much they should get paid to lend to the government for 30 years. That's why the 30-year row wears the flag (⚑): at 5.23% it's higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months. The other flag is a happier one — the equal-weight S&P (every stock counted the same, giant or small) is unusually strong versus its own recent history, which tells you the average stock is holding up well even while headlines focus on the losers. On the plumbing side: the Fed's balance sheet shrank another $14.3B this week as it keeps letting bonds roll off, and the old overnight cash buffer (the reverse-repo facility) is essentially empty — which is exactly why announcements about bond supply now move markets more than Fed statements do. There's no cash-market stress anywhere: overnight lending rates are steady at 3.63%.
movers_html:
How this section works: every S&P 500 stock is scanned mechanically (502/502 covered); a stock makes the list only by moving more than 4% (or 2.5% for the 50 biggest companies) — never because it seems interesting. 29 qualified Thursday; the brief shows at most 3 + a sector note, preferring earnings reactions. "Stated reason" is what reporting said, which is not the same as what's true.

WMT −9.15% (103.84, from 114.30) — what happened: Walmart's worst day of the year, on earnings. Stated reason: its slowest quarterly sales growth in more than six years (Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq.com). Why it matters: Walmart sells groceries and basics to more American households than anyone — when its growth stalls, it can be an early read on the whole consumer. But it's one company's quarter, and the same week a luxury name (Estée Lauder) and an equipment maker (Deere) both beat. So: worth watching closely, not worth panicking over — CL-0004 is the watch, with a deadline.

MRNA −23.55% (133.32, from 174.38) — what happened: Moderna gave back about a quarter of its value the day after its record +177% surge. Stated reason: investors taking profits on the cancer-vaccine rally; analysts warned of more swings ahead (Seeking Alpha). Why it matters: honestly, it doesn't — for the economy. It matters as a lesson: this is what a stock looks like after an all-or-nothing event (a drug trial) pays off — a huge pop, then a violent argument about what the win is actually worth. Clients will ask about it; the answer is about position sizing, not prediction.

DE +6.94% (620.94, from 580.63) — what happened: Deere's best day among this week's earnings reporters. Stated reason: quarterly profit of $1.38B on sales up 5% to $12.6B, both better than expected, and it raised the bottom of its full-year forecast; construction-equipment sales grew 18% while its big row-crop farm-equipment business shrank 6% (Bloomberg, GuruFocus). Why it matters: companies buying construction equipment is real-economy investment happening now — it rhymes with Thursday's hot factory survey. The soft spot (large-scale farming) has been in its own recession for a while. The economy this paints: growing overall, with specific weak pockets — the same picture Walmart-versus-Estée-Lauder paints on the consumer side.

Sector note: for the first time since this system began, no sector moved 1.5+ points away from the market — Thursday's selling hit everything roughly equally. After two days of money rotating between sectors, that uniformity means Thursday was about reducing risk overall (because rates rose), not about picking new winners and losers.
chart_of_day_why: The 30-year Treasury yield is the single number driving everything this week — the AI-stock selloff, the sector rotation, Thursday's broad decline. The chart shows its climb over six months; the marks are Monday's 5.31% peak and Wednesday's 5.19% dip after the Treasury's buyback announcement. Thursday closed halfway back at 5.23%. (Selected by rule: it carries the morning's biggest ⚑ flag.)
tier3_html:
The week in review (Friday depth): the AI-chip group had a whiplash week. Versus the S&P: 3.4 points worse Tuesday, 1.8 points worse Wednesday — then 1.2 points better Thursday while the market fell. Even after all that, the group is up 56.2% this year against the market's 11.8%. Inside the group, the swings were wildest in the specialist suppliers — fiber-optics maker Coherent fell 12.8% Tuesday, storage maker Seagate lost 16.3% in two days, then similar names led Thursday's bounce. A trade that everyone had piled into got violently unwound and partially re-bought inside four sessions. On the evidence so far, that's about crowded positioning, not about anyone canceling AI orders — the formal test (CL-0002) settles Tuesday.

The financing watch — why this section exists: the AI buildout is increasingly funded with borrowed money, and history's tech busts (the dot-com telecom collapse especially) started in exactly that kind of financing, not in the products. The standing item: Bank of America last week sized one new Broadcom-linked financing vehicle at a possible $370B of debt by 2029 — a structure that borrows money to buy chips and lease them to AI companies. This week's scoreboard: AI stocks repriced violently, but AI-related credit didn't blink, and no lender pulled back. Stock volatility with calm credit is what the early-to-mid stage of a financing cycle looks like. The moment credit stops being calm is the moment this section starts shouting — that's the thing it watches for every week.

Liquidity check (weekly): the Fed's balance sheet shrank $14.3B to $6.746T (its slow, planned wind-down continues), the government's checking account sits at $954B, the overnight cash buffer is empty, and overnight lending rates are steady. Plain version: there's no shortage of cash in the banking system — the pressure on long-term rates this week came from supply-and-demand for long bonds, not from money getting tight day-to-day.

calendar_note_html: A quiet calendar: just the flash PMIs — early monthly survey readings of business activity (anything above 50 = growing; expectations are ~54). After Thursday's blowout factory survey, the risk runs one way: weak readings would be shrugged off, but strong ones would push long-term rates higher still. Today's close also settles CL-0001.
concept_unit: Unit 1 · Yield curve mechanics · segment 3 of ~10
concept_title: Naming the move: steepeners, flatteners, and what each one says
concept_html: Bond people compress every move in interest rates into a two-word name, and this week is a perfect chance to learn the vocabulary on live examples. Word one is direction: bull means yields fell (good for bondholders — prices rise), bear means yields rose. Word two is shape: a steepener means the gap between long and short rates widened; a flattener means it narrowed. Monday was a bear steepener: long yields jumped while short ones sat still — the market demanding more pay to hold long bonds, historically the most uncomfortable backdrop for stocks. Wednesday was a bull flattener: long yields fell 9bp on the Treasury's buyback news while short rates didn't move. Thursday, the bear steepener crept back. Here's the payoff of the vocabulary: the name tells you who moved, and who moved tells you what the market is thinking. When short rates drive, investors are re-voting on the Fed. When long rates drive — as they did all week — the vote is about long-term supply and required compensation, and the Fed is just a spectator. The 2-year's total range this week: zero. That's how you know which conversation the market is having.
client_translation: "All the drama in bonds this week happened in 20- and 30-year paper — short rates never moved. Markets aren't arguing about what the Fed does next; they're arguing about what it should cost to lend the government money for decades."
client_lens_html:
• "Walmart was down 9% — is the consumer rolling over?" — The honest answer: one flagship warning sign, actively being tested. Walmart's growth is the slowest in six years, but the same week a luxury brand beat and raised and Deere's construction business grew 18%. Tell clients what would confirm real softness (other consumer names following) rather than delivering a verdict early.
  • "Moderna went up 177% and then dropped 24% — should we chase it?" — Both moves are the same event: the market repricing a coin flip that already landed, then arguing over the payout. The only part an investor ever controls is how much they bet before the flip — that's the position-sizing conversation, and this week hands you the perfect illustration.
  • "Why do my bond funds keep swinging?" — Because long-term rates moved sharply three times this week (5.31 → 5.19 → 5.23 on the 30-year) while short-term rates didn't move at all. Short-duration holdings — money markets, short CDs, short bond funds — slept through the whole thing. It's a concrete week for explaining that the risk decision in bonds isn't whether to own them, it's how long you lend for.
